# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
**Summary as I read it:** this is the registered two-year follow-up of the Varden trial, plus 14 Halden organisations that hold output records.
- **Varden case-processing offices:** the per-hour gain fell from 12.5% to 9.8% on timesheets, and stands at 8.5% on stricter system-log hours (CI 3.4 to 13.8). Output per employee is −3.4%.
- **Mediation:** a registered analysis attributes 47% of the gain to fewer recurring meetings and 18% to lower fatigue, leaving 35% unexplained.
- **Counter offices:** the county ended this arm at month 12 because waits were 7.3 versus 4.0 minutes.
- **Halden subset:** 3 of 14 organisations reverted. The 11 that continued show +11.8% per actual hour, which the authors label an upper bound.
- **Earlier claims:** the report rebuts the "entirely artifact" claim and the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim.

The arithmetic reconciles: 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8%, 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5%, 96.8 / 0.866 = +11.8%, and the confidence intervals are symmetric on the log scale. The report also settles what I left open after the meta-analysis. It confirms that the four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. Their 14% should therefore be compared with the 18.7% from uncontrolled designs, so they show decline, not its absence.

This is the strongest document in the series, and its central result has earned its weight. **A gain of about 8–9% per hour, measured on records, logs and against a randomised control, still present after two years.** That rules out "entirely an artifact," and it shouldn't be hedged. My main concerns are below. The first could change how the mediation result is read.

## 1. What the log-hours denominator contains decides what the mediation result means

System logs are described as recording "time staff are working on cases." Meetings are not case work. So either:

**(a) Logs exclude meeting time.** In that case the 11% fall in log hours is hard to reconcile with the meeting figures. Relative to control, meetings fell by about 3.3 hours a week, while timesheet hours fell by about 4.5. That leaves non-meeting time down only about 4%, not 11%.

**(b) Logs include meeting time** (for example, staff stay logged in through meetings). Then simple accounting nearly settles the question. Output fell about 3.4% while non-meeting hours fell about 4%, so output per *non-meeting* hour is essentially unchanged, around +1%. That implies **meeting removal accounts for roughly 85–90% of the per-hour gain**, not 47%, and arguably more than the interval's upper limit of 66%. This repeats what I found at nine months, more strongly.

Neither reading fits all the reported numbers. The authors should report **log hours and timesheet hours as levels**, say whether meetings appear in the logs, and explain how a mediation share of 47% sits alongside the accounting decomposition. Even if (b) is right, the gain is not an artifact. Removing hours that produce no cases is a genuine productivity gain. But it changes what the gain *is*. It would be mostly reorganisation, with rest playing a small part.

There is a related loose inference. "Log data show slightly more work than timesheets" is drawn from a *smaller percentage fall* in log hours. That doesn't show unrecorded work unless the levels are compared.

## 2. Like-for-like comparisons

- **The summary mixes measures.** "Fell from 12.5% … to 8.5%" compares nine-month timesheet hours with 24-month log hours. The like-for-like change is 12.5% to 9.8%. That is a fall of about a fifth on the log scale, not a third. The body gets this right; the summary should match it.
- **The decline isn't tested.** The nine- and 24-month intervals overlap almost completely. "Consistent with some fading" is the right wording. In §5, "declined by about a quarter" states a point-estimate difference as if it were established.

## 3. Mediation wording and inference

- **"Confirms" is stronger than "survives a registered test."** Mediation in a cluster trial rests on the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption the authors acknowledge.
- **The effective sample size is still 14 clusters.** "A larger sample of office-months" overstates the gain in precision, because months within an office aren't independent. The interval of 28–66% may be optimistic if the standard errors don't account for clustering.
- **The analysis is not fully out of sample.** The hypothesis came from month-6 data, and the 24-month outcome presumably includes those early months. Registering at month 11 protects the model specification but not the data.
- **Source of the baseline meeting figures.** The nine-month report said meeting data were collected only in month six. The baseline figures here (7.4 and 7.2) must be retrospective calendar data. That's probably fine, but the source should be stated.

## 4. The control-office meeting audit has two implications the report doesn't draw out

- **Contamination.** Two of the seven control offices cut meetings from month 15, probably prompted by the trial's own published finding. This narrows the treated–control gap for months 15–24. The 24-month estimate is therefore somewhat conservative as a measure of the full package. That should be stated in the limitations.
- **It is per-worker evidence.** These offices kept their hours unchanged, so a 4.1% rise in output per hour is a 4.1% rise in **output per worker**. That is the figure an employer cares about, and the trial's arms never produce it. On its face, reorganisation alone raised output per worker, while reorganisation plus fewer hours lowered it by 3.4%. It is two offices with a before–after comparison, open to seasonality and regression to the mean, and the authors rightly don't lean on it. But it makes the missing arm — reorganisation without reducing hours — the obvious next trial.

## 5. Counter-office costing

The county's estimate of 12% more staff appears to assume that the 6.7% per-hour gain would survive restaffing. At nine months I suggested that gain was largely higher utilisation from longer queues. If so, it would disappear once waits returned to normal, and actual hours alone imply about **20% more staff** (37.6 / 31.2). A cost increase of 9% per contact is then probably a lower bound.

## 6. The Halden subset and authorship

- **Selection.** Calling the 11 continuing organisations an upper bound for self-selected adopters is honest. Note the extra layer: 9 of 23 organisations didn't respond, on top of attrition and reversion.
- **The marketing agency's reversion matters.** It is "discretionary" under the meta-analysis's coding, yet it reverted over client deadlines. That supports the meta-analysis's own limitation: the coverage/discretionary distinction is about how a role responds to external demand, not about sector. Client-facing deadline work behaves partly like coverage work.
- **Attrition.** R. Okafor co-authors this report. Section 5 credits the re-analysis on measurement but doesn't acknowledge its finding that the Halden working paper misreported when and why organisations withdrew. A sentence correcting the record would strengthen the report's credibility.

## Where the series now stands

- **Settled (in one public employer, randomised, over two years):**
  - Output per hour in backlog work rises about 8–10% relative to control, and the gain persists with modest fading.
  - Output per worker is slightly lower.
  - In coverage-bound work, the cost was high enough that the county ended the arm.
- **Supported:** reduced meeting time is a major source of the gain. It is at least about half by the mediation model, and possibly most of it, depending on point 1. Fatigue contributes but is secondary.
- **Open:**
  - Whether reorganisation *without* an hours cut captures most of the gain. The control-office audit hints that it might; the counter-hypothesis is that the hours cut is what makes reorganisation happen and stick.
  - Effects beyond 24 months.
  - Private-sector and production settings.

The most informative next study is a three-arm trial: reduced hours, a meeting and workflow audit at full hours, and control. I can sketch that design, or draft the questions for the authors, starting with the log-hours definition, since that point decides how the mediation result should be read.
